clue.text: Very funny comedian marked on map with 9

blocks.note: a killing joke is hilariously funny
W. C. Fields, the American film comedian

explanation.surface: A hilarious comic somehow ends up plotted on a map beside a symbol.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer 9 is CROSSED SWORDS, the map symbol for the site of a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Battle sites carry the crossed-swords symbol on maps, and grounds of slaughter are exactly such places.

clue.text: Cross about bungled raid? Make it clear

blocks.note: cross means angry
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An angry reaction to a botched police raid, with a demand to explain it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a verb or a shape, but here it is the adjective meaning angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To irradiate is to shine light upon something, illuminating it so it becomes bright and visible.

clue.text: Composer for the single harmonica

blocks.note: the last two letters of single run into the first three of harmonica

explanation.surface: A composer writing a piece for solo harmonica.
explanation.walkthrough: The name sits across the join of singLE HARmonica. Franz Lehar was the Austro-Hungarian composer of The Merry Widow.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehar wrote operettas, most famously The Merry Widow, so he is an example of a composer.

clue.text: Crosses alternative shotgun out

explanation.definitionFit: In the game of noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe) one player marks O symbols, the other player marks X symbols.

clue.text: Buddy ornament for old city amid ships

indicators.note: amid places one item in the middle of another, enclosed by it

blocks.note: a fleet is a group of ships
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: A trinket bought for a friend in an ancient port full of vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buddy' looks like 'friend', but it means full of buds.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleuret is a small decorative flower motif, so an ornament shaped like buds and blooms.

clue.text: I lost out entering poem consisting of letters

indicators.note: out means the words are put out of order and so rearranged

blocks.note: the five letters to rearrange
an epic is a long narrative poem

explanation.surface: A poet confesses to losing their way while composing a verse work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' does double service here as a jumbling signal, not a statement that something is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a letter, so a work described this way is made up of written correspondence.

clue.text: Information: I'm not sure when I heard it ...

indicators.note: heard means we go by what the ear catches, not the written spelling

blocks.note: when is a date, and um is the hesitation noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: Someone groping to recall when they picked up a piece of news.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, 'date, um?' runs together into the singular of data.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is a single item of fact or a given figure, the singular of data.

clue.text: French tea, nuts and porridge, less thrilling to Wordsworth

blocks.note: the is the French word for tea
both mean crazy
porridge and bird are both British slang for a prison sentence

explanation.surface: A breakfast menu of tea, nuts and oats that a Romantic poet found dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem To the Cuckoo asks 'O Cuckoo! shall I call thee Bird, Or but a wandering Voice?' — the poet was more thrilled by the voice than the mere bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's poem prefers the bird's wandering voice to the creature itself, which inspires him less.

clue.text: Quarrelled with news-papermen among these

indicators.note: among puts one group in the middle of another, enclosed by it

blocks.note: these refers to the puzzles the solver is doing
editors, the men who run newspapers

explanation.surface: An argument among journalists about the puzzles in their paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'These' points at the very puzzles you are solving; the editors sit inside CROSS-WORDS.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross swords with someone is an idiom for arguing or clashing with them.

clue.text: Stag at bingo, would-be seducer in 13

blocks.note: a hart is a male deer
house is the old name for bingo, and the winner's call

explanation.walkthrough: 13 is HARD TIMES, the Dickens novel; James Harthouse tries to seduce Louisa Bounderby in it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the novel James Harthouse is the idle gentleman who attempts to lure the unhappily married Louisa away.

clue.text: Wearing Sikh headgear, monarch comes in between cities

Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.walkthrough: The monarch goes in just after the first letter of the headgear, splitting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Inter- means among, and urban relates to towns, so an interurban route links separate towns and cities.

clue.text: Grace Darling's tree

blocks.note: the end of Grace runs into the start of Darling

explanation.surface: A tree associated with Grace Darling, the Victorian lighthouse heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: The tree belongs to Grace Darling only in the sense that it lies in her name: graCE DARling. She was a lighthouse keeper's daughter famed for a sea rescue in 1838.
explanation.definitionFit: The cedar is a tall evergreen conifer, so it is a straightforward kind of tree.

clue.text: Letters to "Dear Smith" by  ...

indicators.note: the letters of the quoted greeting are to be taken and set out afresh

blocks.note: the nine letters of the greeting

explanation.surface: Correspondence addressed to a Mr Smith, signed by someone named in the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs on into 14: the answer is the novel 'by Charles Dickens'. 'Letters' looks like correspondence but means the letters of the greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is the 1854 novel written by Charles Dickens, so it is a work by that author.

clue.text: ...  writer, Adler's alias, surrounded by birds

indicators.note: an alias is a different name, so the name is disguised by rearrangement

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange
chickens are birds

explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues from 13, so 'writer' is the author of that novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens is the Victorian novelist, the author of Hard Times, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Eleventh hour landing in the sea?

blocks.note: first meaning: made at the final moment, a desperate last attempt
second meaning, playful: a pilot's final ditching of a plane in water

explanation.walkthrough: To ditch is to bring an aircraft down on water, so a final such landing is a whimsical second reading, flagged by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A last-ditch effort is one made at the final possible moment, just as an eleventh-hour attempt is.

clue.text: Agriculture only possible for younger people?

blocks.note: first meaning: cultivation of the land
second meaning, read as two words

explanation.surface: A claim that farming is a job only for the young.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as TILL AGE, the answer describes something allowed only until one reaches a certain age.
explanation.definitionFit: Tillage is the work of ploughing and preparing soil for crops, a core part of farming.

clue.text: Soul is not immortal, I allege, and memory is included

indicators.note: included means put inside, so this word goes within the other

blocks.note: to aver is to assert or allege
read-only memory in a computer
taken as written

explanation.surface: A philosopher asserting, from memory, that the soul dies.
explanation.walkthrough: Averroes, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher, was read as teaching that the individual soul does not survive.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine attributed to Averroes denies personal immortality, holding only one shared intellect endures.

clue.text: Invigilate lines in Old English

indicators.note: in places one item inside another, which wraps round it

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
lines of poetry

explanation.surface: Supervising an exam on poetry written in Anglo-Saxon.
explanation.definitionFit: To invigilate is to supervise candidates during an examination, so to watch over and supervise them.

clue.text: Awfully angered

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the word is mangled into new order

blocks.note: the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight it defines the answer, and it also instructs the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone furious or extremely cross is enraged, which is anger at a very high pitch.

clue.text: See 14
Nothing but stones (Spooner's slow speech expressing irony)

explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of WRY DRAWL to get the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dry wall is built of stones laid without mortar, so it consists only of stones.

clue.text: 25's son-in-law obliged to run into horse-race

indicators.note: run into means the two words run together, sharing a letter where they overlap

blocks.note: bound means obliged
the Derby, the famous flat race at Epsom

explanation.walkthrough: BOUND and DERBY overlap on their shared D. Josiah Bounderby marries Louisa, the daughter of Thomas Gradgrind (25) in Hard Times.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hard Times the banker Bounderby weds Gradgrind's daughter Louisa, becoming his son-in-law.

clue.text: See 11
A load of French snails

blocks.note: escargots, the French dish of snails, kept without its first two and last two letters

explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits at the heart of esCARGOts, the French word for snails.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo is the goods carried by a ship or aircraft, a consignment or freight load.

taken as written

clue.text: Protagonist of 13 gets new grid, about 1,000 pounds

indicators.note: new means made over again, so the letters are freshly arranged

blocks.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds
the letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 13 is Hard Times, so the protagonist is its schoolmaster; a grand is British slang for a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gradgrind, the facts-obsessed schoolmaster, is the central figure of Dickens's novel Hard Times.

clue.text: Not getting anywhere hot, lined off with percussion

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or out of place, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: the eight letters to rearrange
drums are percussion instruments

explanation.surface: A drummer stuck in a hot, stuffy, lined room going nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The doldrums are the calm equatorial belt where sailing ships were becalmed.
explanation.definitionFit: A becalmed ship makes no progress, so the phrase describes stagnation or a slump.
